w: Only the Palace of Mafra in Portugal rivals this place for sheer Benedictine ambition - a monastery so vast it now swallows an entire university humanities department without feeling crowded. Part of the late Baroque ensemble that rebuilt Catania after catastrophe, it reads less like a building than a small stone city.
s: One of Europe's largest Benedictine monasteries
_facts: former Benedictine monastery at Piazza Dante 30
with the Palace of Mafra, ranks among the largest Benedictine monasteries in Europe
part of the late Baroque Val di Noto ensemble; now houses the University of Catania's Department of Humanities

w: Civic power and religious power have faced each other across this square since the city was rebuilt after its last great catastrophe - city hall on one side, the Cathedral of Saint Agatha on the other, with the black lava elephant fountain standing referee between them.
s: Catania's square, church facing city hall
_facts: main city square in Catania, flanked by the city hall at Palazzo degli Elefanti and the Duomo (Cathedral of Saint Agatha)

w: Still a private residence, and still opening its lavishly decorated rooms to anyone who books a guided tour - the Biscari family's palace is one of the few in Catania where you can actually walk the interiors rather than admire the facade from the street.
s: A private palace you can actually tour inside
_facts: monumental private palace in Catania
highly decorative interiors open for guided tours, used for social and cultural events

w: Its full title runs longer than most people's patience - the Ancient Royal and Eminent Basilica Collegiate of Our Lady of the Alms - but everyone just calls it the Collegiata. Finished in 1794, it's textbook Sicilian Baroque: theatrical, over-decorated, utterly unbothered by restraint.
s: Sicilian Baroque under an impossibly long name
_facts: full name Ancient Royal and Eminent Basilica Collegiate of Our Lady of the Alms
finished in 1794, an example of Sicilian Baroque

w: Built in 1768 to celebrate a royal wedding, this lava-and-limestone arch carries a phoenix on one face and a Latin motto that could be Catania's civic slogan: 'Melior de cinere surgo' - better I rise from the ashes. Fitting for a city levelled by lava and earthquake and rebuilt anyway, more than once.
s: A gate whose motto is Catania's whole history
_facts: triumphal arch built 1768, originally Porta Ferdinandea, celebrating the marriage of Ferdinand I to Maria Carolina
built of alternating white Siracusa stone and dark lava blocks; designed by Francesco Battaglia and Stefano Ittar
east-side tympanum bears a phoenix and the motto 'Melior de cinere surgo' (Better I arise from the ashes)

w: Catania's oldest park still goes by its old name, Villa Bellini, honouring the city's opera-composer son - about seven hectares of shaded paths and flowerbeds that have given the city room to breathe since long before anyone thought to call it a heritage garden.
s: Catania's oldest park, named for its composer son
_facts: the oldest urban park of Catania, also known as Villa Bellini
occupies 70,942 square metres

w: Via Crociferi packs three Baroque churches and their convents into a couple of blocks, and San Benedetto anchors the run - a former Benedictine house facing down a onetime Jesuit church across the same narrow street. Walk its length and you get a compressed history of Catania's religious orders.
s: One stop on Via Crociferi's run of Baroque churches
_facts: late-Baroque church and former Benedictine monastery, facade facing Via Crociferi
faces the former Jesuit church of San Francesco Borgia across the street
about a block south of the church and convent of San Giuliano

w: City government has run out of this building, in one form or another, since it was still called the Loggia Senatoria - its current Baroque skin just the latest version of a town hall that has watched over Piazza del Duomo, and the elephant fountain, for centuries.
s: Catania's town hall, on the Duomo's Baroque stage
_facts: historical building housing Catania's Town Hall
the prior building was known as the Palazzo Senatorio or Loggia Senatoria

n: Basilica of Our Lady of Mount Carmel
w: Tucked onto Piazza Carlo Alberto, this Marian sanctuary carries minor-basilica status and a mouthful of a formal name - Maria Santissima Annunziata al Carmine - but locals just call it the Carmine, a quieter stop than the Duomo a few streets over.
s: A quieter Marian basilica off Piazza Carlo Alberto
_facts: Roman Catholic minor basilica and Marian sanctuary on Piazza Carlo Alberto, Catania
also called Basilica di Maria Santissima Annunziata al Carmine

w: Monks once filled this Benedictine complex two blocks from the cathedral; now its cloisters hold Catania's State Archives, with another wing given over to cultural exhibitions as the Palazzo della Cultura. The church still stands watch over a piazza that quietly became a records office.
s: A monastery reborn as Catania's state archive
_facts: Roman Catholic church and former Benedictine monastery, two blocks east of Catania Cathedral
part of the convent occupied by the Palazzo della Cultura, used for cultural exhibitions
the Monastero di San Placido now serves as the Archivio di Stato di Catania (State Archives)

w: Sixteen thousand square metres of cultivated green run by the university's botany department - a working research garden as much as a public one, cataloguing Mediterranean and exotic flora under an international registry code most visitors never notice on their way to smell the roses.
_facts: 16,000 sqm botanical garden operated by the University of Catania's botany department
a member of BGCI (Botanic Gardens Conservation International), international identification code CAT

w: Half the square hosts markets, the other half is Roman ruins - the sunken remains of Catania's amphitheatre sit where a Bourbon king's statue once stood, before Garibaldi's forces settled that argument in 1861. A monument to opera composer Vincenzo Bellini took the plinth instead, opera characters and all.
s: Roman ruins sharing a square with the market
_facts: rectangular square in the historic centre, frequently hosts markets, bisected by Via Etna
western half displays ruins of Catania's former Roman amphitheatre, faced by the neoclassical church of San Biagio
an 1842 guide records a monument to King Ferdinand II here, removed after the 1861 Bourbon defeat and replaced with a monument to composer Vincenzo Bellini

w: The family that built this Baroque palace still lives in part of it - the rest has become a hotel, while the piazza outside, once home to a girls' education institute and now mostly a parking lot, still hides a civic art gallery inside a former church at its edge.
s: A Baroque palace its own family never fully left
_facts: Baroque monumental palace in Piazza Manganelli, still lived in by heirs of the family, also houses a hotel
piazza once housed the Istituto per la Educazione delle Fanciulle (Institute for Education of Girls), now mainly a parking lot
a civic art gallery occupies the former church of San Michele Minore at the piazza's north end

w: Raised in 1900 in full Liberty style, Italy's answer to Art Nouveau, this stage has hosted cinema, song and drama for over a century, and now shares ownership with the grander Teatro Massimo Bellini across town. Its ironwork facade still faces down the Baroque bulk of Palazzo Manganelli across the street.
s: A 1900 Liberty-style stage facing a Baroque palace
_facts: cinematography, song and drama stage erected 1900, opposite the Palazzo Manganelli
designed in Liberty style (Italian Art Nouveau)
presently owned by the same entity as the Teatro Massimo Bellini

w: The oversized windows on the top floor gave surgeons daylight to operate by back in 1904 - the whole point of the design. A century on, the Liberty-style building has traded scalpels for spreadsheets as a bank's offices, but the windows built for surgery still flood the upper floor with light.
s: A surgery built for daylight, now a bank
_facts: former surgical facility on Viale Regina Margherita, erected 1904, designed by Carlo Sada in Liberty style
presently houses offices of the Intesa San Paolo bank
remarkable for large upper-floor windows built to provide natural light for the surgical suite

w: Black lava at the base, white stone pillars framing it - vintage Vaccarini, the architect who shaped Baroque Catania. Its striking feature is a 1920 bronze honouring the duke's son, a volcano-obsessed geologist who studied Etna and Vesuvius, then was exiled and jailed by the Bourbons for his politics.
s: A Baroque palace honouring an exiled scientist
_facts: palace attributed to architect Giovanni Battista Vaccarini, base of dark lava stone framed with white stone pillars, completed 1743 for Duke Gioeni d'Angio
bronze monument (completed 1920 by Mario Rutelli) honours Giuseppe Gioeni d'Angio, the duke's son, a geologist who studied the volcanoes of Campania and Sicily
Giuseppe was exiled and later imprisoned by Bourbon authorities for his political activity during the Napoleonic era

w: A car showroom wrapped in gilded mosaics and grotesque face masks, with a baron's apartment stacked on top - Fascist-era rationalist architects loathed its flamboyant Liberty style on principle. It's still selling car parts on the ground floor, under decoration extravagant enough to have scandalised the whole movement.
s: A car showroom too flamboyant for the Fascists' taste
_facts: Liberty-style building at Piazza Bovio housing an automobile showroom below and Baron Musumeci's apartments above, designed by Francesco Fichera
design maligned during the Fascist era by critic Pietro Maria Bardi and the MIAR rationalist architects
facade has a chamfered corner balcony, colourful gilded mosaics and face masks; ground floor still sells car parts today

w: A black basalt elephant has stood at the dead centre of Catania since the 1730s, and everyone just calls it 'u Liotru' - the city's mascot, its origin half-legend, its silhouette on every souvenir in town. Vaccarini built the whole Baroque square around this one stubborn beast.
s: Catania's basalt elephant mascot since the 1730s
_facts: monument designed by Giovanni Battista Vaccarini, 1735-1737, in the centre of Piazza del Duomo
main element a black basalt statue of an elephant, known as 'u Liotru'
has become the emblem of the city of Catania
